extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent applicants (Asian Member States / AMS)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting and examining patent claims and specifications with respect to clarity, allowable claim types, claim support, claim format, and sufficiency of disclosure for AMS (Asian Member States). Focuses on what makes claims clear, supported and enabled for a Person Skilled In the Art (PSIA).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of claim language (PSIA standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the terms of a claim must be clear for a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA) from the wording of the claim alone. Clarity must be analysed in light of the application disclosure, teachings of the prior art, and the claim interpretation a PSIA would give at the time the invention was made. If a PSIA can determine the boundaries of the claimed invention with a reasonable degree of certainty, the claim complies with clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider claim wording together with specification and prior art. Breadth alone does not imply lack of clarity. Raise an objection when a PSIA cannot determine boundaries with reasonable certainty (PCT ISPE GL refs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent claims must specify essential features
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention, except insofar as such features are implied by the generic terms used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a claim to a 'bicycle' need not mention 'wheels'. Ensure essential technical features are present or clearly implied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity applies to individual claims and the claim set
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement that the claims should be clear applies both to individual claims and to the set of claims as a whole, irrespective of product, process or product-by-process claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity both for each claim and for how claims interact as a set; inconsistencies among claims can create clarity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims producing a product must necessarily result in that product
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim relates to a process for producing the product of the invention, the process as claimed should be one which, when carried out in a manner which would seem reasonable to a PSIA, necessarily results in that particular product; otherwise there is internal inconsistency and lack of clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check that recited process steps, when reasonably performed, produce the claimed product. If not, object for inconsistency/lack of clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims defining modified known products must identify modifications
rubrics_metrics.description: In the case of a product claim where the product is of a well-known kind and the invention lies in modifying it, it is sufficient if the claim clearly identifies the product and specifies what is modified and in what way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure clear identification of the base product and clear specification of the modification (similar considerations apply to apparatus claims).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms not allowed — vague, relative or ambiguous wording
rubrics_metrics.description: Terms that may be regarded as ambiguous, inadequate, unclear, or too broad include indefinite/relative words (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong'), terms of approximation (e.g., 'about', 'approximately'), ambiguous adverbs/phrases (e.g., 'preferably', 'more preferably', 'in particular', 'substantially', 'mostly', 'similarly', 'for example', 'such as'), references to parts of the description, trademarks/trade names/proper names, and multiple outcomes (e.g., 'and/or').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such terms may lead to lack of clarity and should be avoided unless they have a well-recognised meaning in the art or the description provides a standard for measurement. Examiner should determine if PSIA would be apprised of meaning from description or prior art; invite applicant to define or excise ambiguous terms if not supported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms of degree require disclosed measurement standards
rubrics_metrics.description: If a term of degree (e.g., 'thin') appears in a claim, the examiner should determine whether the PSIA would be apprised of the meaning either by disclosure of a standard for measuring that degree in the description or in view of the prior art and state of the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no standard is provided and PSIA would not know the meaning, raise an objection; provide concrete measuring conditions/numerical limits in description where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions like 'preferably' generally non-limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions like 'preferably', 'for example', 'such as' or 'more particularly' should generally be regarded as having no limiting effect on the scope of a claim; the feature following such an expression should be regarded as optional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious when applicants try to rely on such expressions to limit claims; consider them non-limiting unless the description explicitly states otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant cannot rely on unclear terms to distinguish from prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant cannot rely on an unclear or ambiguous term to distinguish the claimed invention from the prior art. It may be appropriate to invite the applicant to define or remove the term without extending subject-matter beyond the content as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant uses vagueness to evade prior art, require definition or amendment supported by the original disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Result-to-be-achieved type claims allowed only if verifiable and achievable
rubrics_metrics.description: No objection should be raised if the invention can only be defined in result terms, so long as the result is one which can be achieved without undue experimentation and can be directly and positively verified by tests or procedures adequately specified in the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require concrete verification methods in the description. Example distinction: vague 'low roughness' vs numerically defined roughness accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining product by parameters acceptable if parameters measurable and recognised
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition of a product solely by its parameters may be appropriate where invention cannot be defined otherwise, provided that these parameters can be clearly and reliably determined either by indications in the description or by objective procedures recognised in the art. Same applies to process-related features defined by parameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parameters not recognised in the art or measured by non-accessible apparatus may be objectionable. Watch for applicants using unusual parameters to disguise lack of novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims defining relationship to non-claimed second product require caution
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim seeks to define an invention by reference to features of the use or relationship to a second product not part of the claimed invention, lack of clarity can result unless the claim sets forth a clear definition of the individual product being claimed or is directed to a combination of the two products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider substituting wording (e.g., 'connectable' instead of 'connected') or recast as combination claims (e.g., 'engine with a cylinder head').

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate treatment of approximate words ('about')
rubrics_metrics.description: Particular attention is required whenever the word 'about' or similar terms are used (applied to values or ranges). Examiner should judge whether the meaning is sufficiently clear in context. If 'about' prevents unambiguous distinction from prior art, raise objection on novelty or inventive step grounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use context and specification to determine scope; request numeric tolerances or measurement methods where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trademarks and trade names generally lack clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Trademarks and similar expressions that characterise commercial origin rather than properties of goods relevant to the invention are usually considered to lack clarity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invite applicant to remove trademarks from claims unless unavoidable or generally recognised with precise meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimers and negative limitations (limitations in claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be limited by a disclaimer or negative limitation (e.g., 'composition free of water'). Negative limitation is not ambiguous per se, but renders a claim unclear when it attempts to claim by excluding what applicant did not invent rather than reciting what was invented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negative limitations are acceptable where each recited limitation is clear or where alternative elements are positively recited in the description and can be excluded. The mere absence of a positive recitation is not a basis for exclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness — avoid unduly multiplied or duplicative claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims may be objected to as lacking conciseness when they are unduly multiplied or duplicative. The number of claims must be considered in relation to the nature of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claim count relative to invention's complexity. PCT ISPE GL §5.42 applies mutatis mutandis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives in a single claim allowed if not obscure and unity met
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may refer to alternatives provided the number and presentation of alternatives in a single claim does not make the claim obscure or difficult to construe and provided the claim meets the requirements of unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure alternatives are presented clearly and do not cause interpretive ambiguity; consider limiting number of alternatives in one claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for drawings and figure references
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings should be briefly described (e.g., 'Figure 1 is a plan view...'). When referring to elements, use element name and number (e.g., 'resistor 3 is connected to capacitor 5 via switch 4') and ensure description and drawings are consistent in reference numbers and signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow AMS-specific rules for drawings; ensure consistency between description and drawings to avoid clarity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple dependent claims — formatting and grouping
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple dependent claims (dependent on more than one other claim) are allowed in the AMS. They include all limitations contained in the claims to which they relate. Dependent claims should be grouped together practically to enable association of related claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two alternative office practices: (1) require multiple dependent claim to refer only alternatively and prevent multiple dependent claims forming basis for other multiple dependent claims; or (2) allow reference alternatively or cumulatively and allow multiple dependent claims to be basis for other multiple dependent claims. Group dependent claims for readability and easy construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-part claims (two-part form) preferred by many AMS
rubrics_metrics.description: Two-part claiming sections the claim into two parts separated by phrases like 'characterised in that' or 'characterised by': the pre-characterising part describes the prior art features necessary for definition; the characterising portion states the technical features the invention adds to the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First part should indicate the designation and prior-art features relevant to the invention (only those relevant). Second part should state the novel technical features. Use two-part form unless it would give a distorted or misleading picture of the invention or prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Number of independent claims — general permissiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Most AMS do not limit the number of independent claims. Several independent claims in the same category directed to interrelated subject-matter may meet unity even if they appear quite different, provided technical features making a contribution over the prior art are the same or corresponding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess unity based on contribution-making technical features; offices may still consider claim count in relation to nature of invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use claims — equivalence to process claims for examination
rubrics_metrics.description: Use claims are allowed in most AMS (with some exceptions). For examination a 'use of substance X as an insecticide' is regarded as equivalent to a 'process' claim 'process of killing insects using substance X' and is not to be interpreted as directed to a composition per se or to building an apparatus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret use claims as process claims for examination purposes; be mindful of jurisdictional exceptions (e.g., Lao PDR and Viet Nam).

rubrics_metrics.name: Product-by-process claims — treatment and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Product-by-process claims are allowed in all AMS. Where a claim defines a product by the process making it, the claim is directed to the product. Such a claim lacks novelty if an identical product (even if made by undisclosed process) exists in prior art. If the product can only be defined by process steps or the process imparts distinctive characteristics, the examiner should consider the process steps when searching and assessing patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If product can only be defined by process or process imparts unique properties, include process in search/assessment. Example: welding produces properties distinguishing the product; novelty assessed accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ranges in claims — anticipation and selection inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of ranges in claims is explicitly allowed in certain AMS. A specific example in prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range. If a prior-art range overlaps/touches claimed range, novelty depends on case-specific factors; a narrow selected range may be novel if it is not merely an obvious carrying out of prior teaching and shows unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires prior-art disclosure with sufficient specificity. Consider whether the claimed narrow range yields unexpected results (supporting novelty/inventive step) and examine overlap/touching ranges on a case-by-case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imprecise terms and transitional phrases guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims with vague/equivocal wording that leave reader in doubt should be objected for lack of clarity. 'Comprising' is open-ended and allowed; 'consisting of' is closed-ended and allowed; 'characterised by' is allowed in two-part claims. Terms like 'about', 'approximately', 'somewhat' are usually not allowed as they make claims unclear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer clear transitional phrases appropriate to intent. Discourage vague qualifiers unless context/description makes them unambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of claims allowed — product, process, product-by-process, use
rubrics_metrics.description: Product, process and product-by-process claims are allowed in all AMS, and use claims are allowed in most AMS. All applications should contain one or more independent main claims directed to essential features, with reasonable dependent claims claiming specific forms of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognise two basic kinds of claim: product (physical entity) and activity (process/use). Permit reasonable dependent claims even if dependent claim features could be inventions themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be supported by the description and drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be fully supported by the description. There must be a basis in the description for the subject-matter of every claim and the scope of the claims may not be broader than justified by the description and drawings. Support must relate to claimed features; vague statements with no technical content do not provide basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Object for lack of support only when well-founded reasons exist, and where possible support objections with published documents. Treat clarity/support separately from novelty/inventive step and sufficiency of disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendment of claims requires corresponding amendment of description
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendment of a claim should be supported by the description and be clear and concise in order to meet the requirement of clarity; amendment of a claim may require amending the description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicants amend claims, ensure description is amended as needed to maintain consistency and clarity (PCT ISPE GL cross-reference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of disclosure — enabling disclosure standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application is sufficiently disclosed if it provides enough details to enable a PSIA to carry out the invention. All AMS require a specification that sufficiently discloses the invention. Some AMS additionally require disclosure of the 'best mode' of carrying out the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require detailed description of at least one way of carrying out the invention, together with drawings if any. Do not require well-known ancillary features; but ensure all features essential for carrying out the invention are disclosed in sufficient detail so a PSIA can put the invention into practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant responsibility for sufficiency and method details for parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the applicant's responsibility to supply a description meeting disclosure requirements. If claims define invention in terms of parameters, the application must include a clear description of methods used to determine parameter values unless PSIA would know which method to use or unless all methods yield the same result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If methods for measuring parameters are non-obvious or not known to PSIA, require explicit description of measurement procedures in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insufficiency cannot be cured by post‑filing additions
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiner considers disclosure insufficient, the deficiency cannot be cured after filing by adding further examples or features that introduce subject‑matter extending beyond the content as filed. Remedy may be to restrict claims to embodiments sufficiently described and delete other embodiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advise applicants to rely only on what is supported by the filing; corrective amendments should not add new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objections for lack of sufficiency require serious doubts substantiated by facts
rubrics_metrics.description: An objection of lack of sufficient disclosure presupposes serious doubts which are substantiated by verifiable facts. The invention should be described in terms of structure and also function unless functions are immediately apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide verifiable evidence when alleging insufficiency. Avoid speculative objections; refer to concrete failures of reproducibility or lack of enabling detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factors in determining undue experimentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to be considered in determining whether undue experimentation is needed include: (i) breadth of the claims; (ii) nature of the invention; (iii) general knowledge of PSIA; (iv) level of predictability in the art; (v) amount of direction provided in the application (including references to prior art); and (vi) amount of experimentation required to carry out the claimed invention on the basis of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these factors case-by-case to assess whether disclosure enables practice without undue effort. Refer to PCT ISPE GL 5.48-5.51 for more detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irreparable insufficiency examples — chance-dependent and impossible inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two instances of essentially irreparable insufficiency: (a) successful performance depends on chance (results not reproducible or success totally unreliable), and (b) successful performance is inherently impossible because contrary to established physical laws (e.g., perpetual motion machine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between acceptable rates of failure (manufacturing yield issues) versus fundamental non-reproducibility. Where success is impossible or non-reproducible, reject for insufficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in sufficiency objections
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule the burden of proof lies with the party raising the objection. If there are serious doubts about performing the invention, the burden of proof or a demonstration that success is credible rests with the applicant or patent proprietor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require objecting party to substantiate serious doubts; if substantive doubts exist, request applicant to demonstrate credibility (e.g., experimental data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode disclosure requirement in some AMS
rubrics_metrics.description: Some AMS (Cambodia, Malaysia, Myanmar, Thailand) require that the specification set forth the best mode of carrying out the invention contemplated by the inventor, in addition to enabling disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants filing in these jurisdictions must disclose best mode; examiners should verify whether best mode requirement is met where applicable.
